description: Test your knowledge of PA G2 | Inflammation & Healing.

cards.text: Define acute inflammation and explain why sterile injury (e.g., myocardial infarction) causes the same inflammatory response as infection.
cards.answer: Acute inflammation is a rapid protective vascular and cellular response to injury, infection, or abnormal stimuli. It is NOT synonymous with infection; sterile injury triggers identical mechanisms because the body responds to tissue damage itself, not just microorganisms.

tip.tip: Remember: inflammation ≠ infection. Both activate the same vascular cascade.

cards.text: List the five cardinal signs of acute inflammation and identify which is NOT part of Celsus's original description.
cards.answer: Rubor (redness), tumor (swelling), calor (heat), dolor (pain), and functio laesa (loss of function). Functio laesa was added by Virchow; Celsus described only the first four.

tip.tip: Celsus: four signs. Virchow added the fifth (functio laesa = broken function).

cards.text: Which mediators cause vasodilation in acute inflammation, and which vascular beds are affected?
cards.answer: Histamine, nitric oxide (NO), and prostaglandins cause vasodilation. Arterioles dilate first, followed by capillary bed opening, affecting the microcirculation.

tip.tip: HNP: Histamine, NO, Prostaglandins. Remember: arterioles dilate before capillaries.

cards.text: Describe the mechanism of increased vascular permeability via endothelial cell contraction and state which vessel type is primarily affected.
cards.answer: Histamine and leukotrienes cause cytoskeletal contraction in endothelial cells, widening inter-endothelial gaps and allowing protein-rich fluid to leak. This mechanism primarily affects venules.

tip.tip: Endothelial contraction = widened gaps = protein leak. Venules are the weak link.

cards.text: Distinguish between exudate and transudate by protein content, mechanism, and a clinical example of each.
cards.answer: Exudate: >3 g/dL protein, caused by increased permeability (active inflammation), e.g., pleural empyema. Transudate: <1 g/dL protein, caused by hydrostatic/oncotic imbalance, e.g., cardiac failure effusion.

tip.tip: Exudate = EX-cessive protein (inflammation). Transudate = TRAnquil fluid (no inflammation).

cards.text: What is margination, and which cell type predominates in the first 6–24 hours of acute inflammation?
cards.answer: Margination is the movement of leucocytes from the axial stream to the vessel periphery as blood stasis develops. Neutrophils predominate in the first 6–24 hours; monocytes predominate after 24–48 hours.

tip.tip: MARGin = edge of vessel. Early = neutrophils; Late = monocytes.

cards.text: Name three mechanisms by which vascular permeability increases and identify which is most common in acute inflammation.
cards.answer: Endothelial cell contraction (most common), direct endothelial injury, transcytosis, and leucocyte-mediated injury. Endothelial cell contraction is the predominant mechanism, affecting venules.

tip.tip: CDTL: Contraction (most), Direct injury, Transcytosis, Leucocyte. Contraction wins in acute.

cards.text: How does stasis contribute to the recruitment of leucocytes in acute inflammation?
cards.answer: Stasis occurs as blood viscosity increases from fluid loss; flow slows and leucocytes move from the axial stream to the vessel periphery (margination), positioning them for rolling and adhesion to endothelium.

tip.tip: Stasis → slow flow → leucocytes slide to edge → ready for rolling adhesion.
